summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 72) and fuel pricing remains supportive of demand reduction, but actual fuel savings are far below the theoretical ceiling and high‑risk sectors continue to drive travel. Public transport ridership is recovering yet remains below pre‑pandemic levels, signalling the need for targeted interventions.

signals.detail: The modelled ceiling of 35.7 M L/week saved is not being realised; only 0.334 M L were saved in the first week of the mandate (~1% of the ceiling). This gap limits the environmental benefit of the WFH policy.

Daily PT trips reached 1.24 M, projecting to ~451 M trips annually—still about 13% below the 2019 level (522 M) and 11% below the 2025 recovery (506 M). Ridership is improving but has not fully rebounded.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction show low WFH adoption (5‑15%) and high mobility scores (85‑95), indicating sustained travel demand and exposure to fuel price volatility, which could pressure operating costs and inflation.

WFH adoption is uneven: public/GLC employees work from home 60% of the time, while construction workers only 5%. This disparity raises equity concerns and limits the overall effectiveness of the remote‑work mandate.

Fuel price remains high (RON95 RM 4.67/L) which discourages private car use, yet the modest actual fuel savings and incomplete PT recovery suggest limited progress toward a durable shift to public or active modes.

recommendation: Introduce a tiered fuel rebate for high‑risk sectors that meet incremental WFH targets (e.g., 20% increase by Q1 2027) and allocate additional subsidies to expand PT frequency on high‑mobility corridors. Simultaneously, launch an equity grant to support remote‑work infrastructure for low‑adoption occupations, aiming for a minimum 30% WFH uptake across all sectors by end‑2027.
